title: Hosted API Demo: Chat/Text Generation Basics - Starlight Finance
summary: Intro/demo of Redwood hosted API focusing on chat/text generation basics. Covered streaming, key params (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), retries/idempotency, rate limiting, and quick notes on security and trials. Customer wants benchmarks (latency/cost) and a short POC. Next steps: send pricing deck, share benchmark script, create trial creds.
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 10:30 AM PST
Duration: ~42m
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Jordan Miles (Redwood CSM - quick intro), Michael Gomez (Starlight Head of ML), Sara Lee (Platform Eng), Jamal Price (CTO)

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Alex from Redwood. Um, quick roll call - Priya, Jordan -
[00:06] Priya Kapoor: Here, hi!
[00:07] Jordan Miles: Yep here.
[00:09] Michael Gomez: Michael here, thanks for doing this.
[00:11] Sara Lee: Sara on my side.
[00:13] Jamal Price: Jamal.
[00:15] Alex Chen: Awesome. So, today we'll walk through Hosted API chat and text gen basics - streaming, request params, some retry behavior, and then Q&A - total about 30-40 minutes, leave time at the end for next steps. Sound good?
[00:25] Jamal Price: Yep good.

[01:02] Priya Kapoor: Ok jumping in - quick architecture slide - Redwood Hosted API is a REST/SDK interface, you call /v1/generate or the chat endpoint. We support streaming so you can flush tokens as they arrive, and then there are server-side policies for retries and fallbacks.
[01:18] Michael Gomez: Can you show streaming in the demo? That's one thing we care about for latency.
[01:22] Priya Kapoor: Totally - I'll demo both streaming and the non-streaming mode.

[02:10] Priya Kapoor: (screen share) Alright here's a sample chat request - messages array with role-system, user, etc. Temperature, top_p, max_tokens are available. Temperature controls randomness; top_p is nucleus sampling. Note on defaults: temperature 0.7, top_p = 1.0, but you can pin them. Also we have streaming via SSE/websocket; example code snippet in Node and Python in the SDK.
[02:45] Michael Gomez: For us most prompts will be constrained - mostly deterministic templates, but we do some creative summarization where we want higher temperature. How does cost change with streaming vs non-streaming?
[02:55] Priya Kapoor: Cost is token based - streaming doesn't change token billing; it's just a different delivery. The main levers for cost are model selection, sequence length (input + output), and quantization/variant if you use smaller variants.

[04:00] Alex Chen: Quick qualifier - what's your current stack? Are you running on-prem models or using an API today?
[04:07] Sara Lee: We use a mix - some internal shorter models for data extraction on-prem, but for customer-facing features we currently call OpenAI. Interested in lowering per-token costs and tighter SLOs.
[04:19] Alex Chen: Got it - something else to note: Hosted API supports model pinning and automatic fallbacks to cheaper model variants if capacity constrained. That can help control cost spikes.

[05:10] Priya Kapoor: Back to the demo - here's streaming in action (starts streaming tokens). The latency to first token in our tests is about 80-120ms on our verified models for typical 2-4 token first-chunk responses, but that depends on region and model.
[05:30] Michael Gomez: 80-120ms? That's the number we're hoping for - what region are you in for that metric?
[05:34] Priya Kapoor: US-West region, and that's with our curated LlamaX-compat models - note sometimes the transcripted names in older docs show 'Llamma' or 'LlaMA' wrong, heh.

[06:20] Jamal Price: On retries - how do retries behave? We have idempotency requirements for some flows.
[06:24] Alex Chen: Great question. On the Hosted API we recommend callers set an idempotency key for non-idempotent workflows. Redwood has client-side retry policies and server-side for transient errors; we surface retryable vs non-retryable errors and the SDK will retry for you by default with exponential backoff, but idempotency keys mean you won't double-process.
[06:45] Sara Lee: Is idempotency key a required header?
[06:47] Priya Kapoor: Optional but recommended. X-Idempotency-Key or SDK helper. If you provide it, we dedupe repeated attempts for the same request within a short window.

[08:00] Priya Kapoor: (shows sample curl) curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat - data {messages: [...], temperature:0.2, max_tokens:256} and if you add "--stream" in the SDK you'll get token deltas back.
[08:25] Michael Gomez: Any guidance on batching? Our traffic pattern is bursty - sometimes spikes to 300 rps for short windows.
[08:33] Priya Kapoor: For Hosted, we do continuous batching on the server side; from a customer perspective you mainly care about concurrency and rate limits. If you need predictable throughput under high RPS, Redwood Dedicated or reserved capacity is recommended; for Hosted we support burst quotas but they can be throttled. We can show you per-route quotas in the console.

[10:05] Alex Chen: Security quick hit - we support SOC 2, SSO/SAML, RBAC, audit logs, and KMS integrations for customer managed keys. Is there anything from a compliance standpoint you need in advance?
[10:16] Jamal Price: We have PCI-adjacent requirements; we need audit logs and VPC peering for some flows.
[10:22] Alex Chen: For PCI-adjacent data, many customers use Private or Dedicated with options for VPC networking. We'll send our security pack; for Hosted we can discuss data retention options and encryption at rest with our KMS integrations.

[11:40] Priya Kapoor: Back to params - a couple of gotchas: max_tokens is for output tokens only in some endpoints, but total token usage for billing is input+output; if you want strict cost caps you can set max_tokens and also implement token counting pre-call. Also top_p and temperature are complementary; setting both can be useful but often people pick one to tune.
[12:15] Michael Gomez: Do you support stop sequences?
[12:18] Priya Kapoor: Yes stop sequences are supported. They work with streaming as well.

[13:30] Sara Lee: Observability - can we get per-token latency and cost breakdown?
[13:34] Alex Chen: Yes, Remote Console shows token-level cost, latency histograms, per-route breakdowns. You can also pull traces via our tracing hooks. We'll share a screenshot and the demo console link.

[15:00] Priya Kapoor: (small demo) Here's the console - route metrics, SLO alerts, and an example rollout: canary to 10% traffic to a cheaper quantized variant, fallback to larger model on errors.
[15:30] Michael Gomez: That fallback behavior - if fallback happens will latencies spike?
[15:33] Priya Kapoor: There's a small hop in latency when switching to a different model variant but we tune routing to prefer models with similar latency profiles. The console shows per-variant latency so you can set fallback policies.

[17:10] Jamal Price: Do you expose raw logs for audit?
[17:14] Alex Chen: Yes audit logs and request/response metadata; for privacy we can suppress full PII in logs or route those to customer-managed logging if required.

[18:50] Michael Gomez: Ok let's talk retries in more depth - if the SDK retries a request and the backend had partially generated tokens, how do you avoid duplicates?
[18:59] Priya Kapoor: Two layers - idempotency on the request side, and server-side dedupe: if a request fails mid-stream we mark it as failed and the SDK can retry with same idempotency-key; the server will either return the previous result or re-run deterministically if the model variant is deterministic (e.g., temperature 0). For non-deterministic settings you should design client idempotency or use logging to reconcile.

[20:40] Sara Lee: For our use case we want deterministic receipts generation - we'll set temperature 0 and pin model. Does Redwood support model pinning?
[20:48] Alex Chen: Yep. Pin a specific model version in the route config on the console and it remains stable until you change it.

[22:00] Priya Kapoor: Walkthrough of a simple benchmark script - Node example calling the chat endpoint with concurrency and recording time to first token and full response times.
[22:25] Michael Gomez: Can you share that script?
[22:27] Priya Kapoor: Yes I'll share the benchmark script and a sample prompt set - we'll also include a spreadsheet with our internal perf numbers for a few representative models.

[24:00] Jamal Price: Any limits on prompt size? We often send 8-10k tokens of context for some analytics features.
[24:08] Priya Kapoor: Hosted models have max context limits depending on the model (e.g., 8k, 32k, etc.). For very large contexts you might consider chunking or using embeddings to pre-filter. We'll ask about your exact sequence lengths.

[26:00] Michael Gomez: On cost - can you do committed pricing or is it purely pay-as-you-go?
[26:07] Alex Chen: Hosted is usage-based; Dedicated/reserved capacity offers committed contracts with predictable throughput and lower effective unit price. For larger volume we can put together a comp based on your forecast.

[28:10] Sara Lee: How do webhooks and streaming integrate - we prefer server-to-server streaming to our ingestion layer.
[28:16] Priya Kapoor: You can use websocket streaming or SSE and then pipe tokens to your ingestion. Some customers write a lightweight aggregation layer to stitch streaming events into final documents. We'll share patterns.

[30:00] Alex Chen: Ok let's do quick recap and next steps. From our side we'll: 1) send pricing deck, 2) share benchmark script + sample prompts, 3) provide security pack (SOC2, KMS and audit logs note), 4) set up trial credentials and a small test project for you.
[30:22] Michael Gomez: That sounds right. We'd also like Redwood to run a quick latency/cost benchmark against our top-3 prompts if possible.
[30:29] Priya Kapoor: We can run an initial bench internally if you share prompts and desired sim load; otherwise we give you the script to run with your traffic profile.

[31:15] Jamal Price: Timeline - we'd like a short POC in 2 weeks. Is that feasible?
[31:18] Alex Chen: Yes, 2 weeks is doable - typical POC includes trial creds, sample data, and 2-3 benchmark runs.

[33:00] Sara Lee: Any gotchas re: network egress or VPC peering?
[33:05] Alex Chen: For Hosted you call our public endpoints; for VPC peering or private networking we'd discuss Private/Dedicated. We'll include networking options in the security pack.

[34:40] Michael Gomez: Are there any throttling policies we need to know about?
[34:45] Priya Kapoor: We have per-account rate limits; you'll see them in the console and we can increase them for POC/test. We also expose retry-after headers on 429s.

[36:10] Alex Chen: Quick note - some older docs call it "KV cash" in transcripts - it should be KV cache, apologies for the audio transcripts.
[36:18] (laughter)

[37:30] Jordan Miles: I'll follow up with a calendar invite for a POC kickoff next week and include the security and trial onboarding notes.

[38:00] Michael Gomez: Great, thanks everyone.
[38:05] Jamal Price: Thanks, appreciate it.
[38:08] Alex Chen: Thanks all - we'll send the deck and scripts by Friday.
[38:12] Priya Kapoor: Thanks, bye.
[38:20] (call ends)
